questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with a history of stable angina presents after an episode of chest pain while shoveling snow. His cardiologist explains that the heart's blood supply is unique compared to other organs. Which of the following best explains why the myocardium is particularly vulnerable to ischemia during sustained tachycardia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The myocardium receives most of its blood supply during systole, and tachycardia disproportionately shortens systole

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tachycardia increases oxygen extraction from coronary blood, which compensates for reduced flow but eventually causes cellular acidosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Coronary blood flow occurs primarily during diastole, and tachycardia shortens diastole while simultaneously increasing myocardial oxygen demand

choices.label: D
choices.text: The coronary arteries lack smooth muscle and therefore cannot autoregulate blood flow during periods of increased heart rate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tachycardia decreases aortic diastolic pressure, which reduces coronary perfusion pressure but does not affect myocardial oxygen demand

explanation.summary: Coronary blood flow occurs primarily during diastole because ventricular contraction during systole compresses coronary vessels. Tachycardia shortens diastole (the filling and perfusion phase), reducing the time available for coronary blood flow, while simultaneously increasing myocardial oxygen demand through more frequent contractions.
explanation.whyCorrect: During systole, ventricular contraction compresses coronary vessels and open aortic valve leaflets block coronary ostia. Most coronary perfusion occurs during diastole. Tachycardia preferentially shortens diastole, reducing coronary perfusion time while the more frequent contractions increase oxygen consumption—a dangerous double threat.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The myocardium receives most of its blood supply during diastole, not systole. During systole, ventricular contraction compresses coronary vessels and reduces flow.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Myocardial oxygen extraction is already near-maximal at rest (70-80%), leaving very little reserve to increase extraction. The heart must increase blood flow, not extraction, to meet increased demand.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Coronary arteries do contain smooth muscle and do autoregulate blood flow. The myogenic response and metabolic vasodilation are key regulatory mechanisms for coronary flow.
whyWrongByChoice.E: While diastolic pressure is relevant to coronary perfusion, tachycardia does increase myocardial oxygen demand. The statement that demand is unaffected is incorrect.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease undergoes a pharmacologic adenosine stress test. During adenosine infusion, he develops substernal chest pain and nuclear imaging reveals a reversible perfusion defect in the inferior wall. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the ischemia observed during this test?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adenosine directly increases myocardial contractility and oxygen demand, overwhelming the oxygen supply in regions with stenotic arteries

choices.label: B
choices.text: Arterioles in ischemic regions are already maximally dilated, while arterioles in healthy regions dilate and divert blood flow away

choices.label: C
choices.text: Adenosine causes vasoconstriction of coronary arteries through alpha-1 adrenergic receptor stimulation, reducing blood flow to all regions

choices.label: D
choices.text: Adenosine reduces systemic blood pressure, causing global myocardial hypoperfusion that preferentially affects the inferior wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: Adenosine closes ATP-sensitive potassium channels in coronary smooth muscle, causing vasoconstriction in the territory of diseased vessels

explanation.summary: This describes coronary steal phenomenon. In coronary artery disease, ischemic regions have arterioles that are already maximally dilated at rest to compensate for reduced flow. Adenosine dilates arterioles in healthy regions but cannot further dilate those in ischemic areas, diverting blood flow away from the ischemic territory.
explanation.whyCorrect: Coronary steal occurs because adenosine causes arteriolar dilation. Arterioles in ischemic regions are already maximally dilated due to chronic metabolic vasodilator release. Healthy regions dilate further in response to adenosine, reducing vascular resistance and pulling blood flow away from the ischemic territory, causing a perfusion defect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adenosine is a vasodilator, not a positive inotrope. It does not directly increase myocardial contractility. The ischemia results from coronary steal, not increased oxygen demand.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Adenosine causes vasodilation, not vasoconstriction. Alpha-1 receptor stimulation is a separate mechanism from the sympathetic nervous system and is easily overridden in coronary arteries.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The ischemia is regional (inferior wall), not global, indicating coronary steal rather than systemic hypoperfusion. The perfusion defect is caused by redistribution of flow, not uniform hypotension.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Adenosine causes vasodilation, not vasoconstriction. When ATP levels are low, KATP channels open causing smooth muscle hyperpolarization and vasodilation, not constriction.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with a history of myocardial infarction presents with exertional chest pain. His cardiologist explains that the heart has a very high arteriovenous oxygen difference compared to other organs. Which of the following values most closely approximates the percentage of oxygen extracted from blood as it passes through the coronary circulation at rest?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 15-20%, similar to the oxygen extraction ratio of renal tissue at rest

choices.label: B
choices.text: 25-30%, similar to the oxygen extraction ratio of resting skeletal muscle

choices.label: C
choices.text: 40-50%, approximately double that of the brain during normal waking activity

choices.label: D
choices.text: 70-80%, the highest of any major organ, reflecting continuous cardiac metabolic demand

choices.label: E
choices.text: 90-95%, leaving virtually no oxygen in coronary venous blood under basal conditions

explanation.summary: The myocardium extracts approximately 70-80% of oxygen from arterial blood at rest, the highest arteriovenous oxygen difference of any major organ. This is because the heart is continuously contracting and has extremely high basal oxygen consumption.
explanation.whyCorrect: The myocardium extracts approximately 70-80% of oxygen at rest, significantly higher than skeletal muscle (25-30%). This high extraction ratio means the heart has very little reserve to increase oxygen extraction and must rely primarily on increasing coronary blood flow to meet additional oxygen demands.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 15-20% is too low for myocardial oxygen extraction. The heart extracts far more oxygen than the kidneys, which receive high blood flow for filtration rather than metabolic needs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 25-30% represents the oxygen extraction of resting skeletal muscle, which is significantly lower than the 70-80% extracted by the myocardium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 40-50% underestimates myocardial oxygen extraction. The heart's continuous contractile activity requires extraction rates of 70-80%.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 90-95% overestimates the extraction. While high, the myocardium extracts approximately 70-80%, leaving coronary venous blood with about 5 mg/dL of oxygen content.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with acute chest pain. Her blood pressure is 152/82 mm Hg and heart rate is 112/min. Troponin levels are elevated, and ECG shows ST depression in leads V4-V6. The attending physician orders intravenous metoprolol. Which of the following best explains how beta-blocker therapy improves the balance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beta-blockers decrease heart rate, prolonging diastole while simultaneously reducing myocardial oxygen consumption

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beta-blockers directly vasodilate coronary arteries by stimulating beta-2 receptors, increasing oxygen delivery to ischemic regions

choices.label: C
choices.text: Beta-blockers increase myocardial contractility, improving cardiac output and increasing coronary perfusion pressure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Beta-blockers primarily act by increasing coronary collateral vessel formation over the first several hours of administration

choices.label: E
choices.text: Beta-blockers increase adenosine production in coronary endothelial cells, causing maximal vasodilation of diseased arterioles

explanation.summary: Beta-blockers reduce heart rate, which prolongs diastole—the phase during which most coronary blood flow occurs. They also reduce myocardial oxygen demand by decreasing heart rate, blood pressure (afterload), and contractility, improving the supply-demand balance.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beta-blockers lower heart rate via beta-1 receptor blockade, prolonging diastole and the time available for coronary perfusion. They simultaneously decrease myocardial oxygen demand by reducing heart rate, contractility, and blood pressure. This dual benefit improves the myocardial oxygen supply-demand balance.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-blockers block beta receptors rather than stimulate them. While beta-2 receptors on coronary vessels mediate vasodilation, beta-blockers would antagonize this effect. The primary benefit is through heart rate reduction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Beta-blockers decrease contractility (negative inotrope), not increase it. Reduced contractility is actually part of how they decrease myocardial oxygen demand.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Collateral vessel formation (angiogenesis) is a chronic process occurring over weeks to months in response to gradual ischemia, not an acute effect of beta-blocker therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Beta-blockers do not directly increase adenosine production. They reduce myocardial oxygen demand, which actually decreases the metabolic signals for vasodilation.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with chronic stable angina undergoes coronary angiography revealing a 90% stenosis of the left anterior descending artery. His cardiologist explains that despite the severe stenosis, he has not had a myocardial infarction because of an adaptive vascular process. Which of the following best describes this protective mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased alpha-1 adrenergic receptor density in coronary arterioles downstream of the stenosis, maintaining perfusion pressure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Upregulation of nitric oxide synthase exclusively within the stenotic segment, preventing further plaque progression

choices.label: C
choices.text: Shift of myocardial metabolism from aerobic to anaerobic glycolysis, reducing dependence on coronary blood flow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Autoregulatory increase in systemic blood pressure to maintain coronary perfusion gradient across the stenosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Development of collateral blood vessels through angiogenesis that partially bypass the stenotic region

explanation.summary: When coronary narrowing occurs slowly and gradually, collateral vessels can form through angiogenesis. These collateral vessels create parallel pathways that partially bypass the stenosis, maintaining some blood flow to the threatened myocardium and preventing infarction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic, gradual coronary narrowing stimulates angiogenesis and the development of collateral vessels within the myocardium. These collaterals create alternative blood supply routes that partially compensate for reduced flow through the stenotic vessel, protecting the myocardium from infarction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-1 receptor stimulation causes vasoconstriction, which would reduce flow rather than maintain it. This would worsen ischemia, not protect against it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: While nitric oxide is an important vasodilator, the protective mechanism is collateral vessel development, not localized upregulation of NO synthase within the stenosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The heart relies primarily on aerobic metabolism and has very limited anaerobic capacity. A shift to anaerobic glycolysis produces insufficient ATP and generates lactate, leading to ischemia and pain rather than adaptation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Systemic hypertension is not a protective autoregulatory response to coronary stenosis. While higher perfusion pressure can partially compensate, it simultaneously increases afterload and myocardial oxygen demand.

questions.stem: A researcher is studying coronary blood flow regulation. She notes that when mean arterial pressure is experimentally increased from 90 mm Hg to 130 mm Hg in an isolated heart preparation, coronary blood flow remains relatively constant. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased nitric oxide release from endothelial cells causes compensatory vasodilation in response to higher perfusion pressure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased adenosine production from myocardial cells triggers arteriolar dilation to match the higher driving pressure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Arterial wall smooth muscle constricts in response to stretch from increased pressure, increasing vascular resistance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Parasympathetic activation causes cholinergic-mediated vasoconstriction in coronary arterioles to limit excess flow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Beta-2 adrenergic receptor downregulation in coronary smooth muscle reduces vasodilatory capacity at higher pressures

explanation.summary: Coronary autoregulation maintains stable blood flow despite changes in perfusion pressure between 70-150 mmHg. The myogenic mechanism is responsible: when arterial pressure increases, vessel wall stretch causes smooth muscle to constrict, increasing resistance and keeping flow relatively constant.
explanation.whyCorrect: Autoregulation of coronary blood flow is mediated by the myogenic response. Increased pressure stretches coronary arterial smooth muscle, which responds by constricting, thereby increasing vascular resistance. Since flow = pressure/resistance, the increased resistance offsets the increased pressure, maintaining stable flow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nitric oxide causes vasodilation, which would decrease resistance and increase flow. This is the opposite of the autoregulatory response needed to maintain constant flow during increased pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Adenosine is released during metabolic demand or ischemia and causes vasodilation. Increased perfusion pressure does not increase adenosine production, and vasodilation would increase rather than maintain flow.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The parasympathetic nervous system has only a minor effect on coronary vessels, causing slight vasodilation rather than vasoconstriction. Autoregulation is primarily a myogenic, not a neural mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Beta-2 receptor downregulation is not a mechanism of coronary autoregulation. Autoregulation occurs through the myogenic response of vascular smooth muscle, independent of adrenergic receptor changes.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with crushing substernal chest pain. Cardiac catheterization reveals complete occlusion of the proximal right coronary artery. The attending explains that the subendocardium is most vulnerable to ischemic injury. Which of the following best explains why the subendocardium is more susceptible to ischemia than the epicardium?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The subendocardium experiences greater compressive forces during systole from ventricular chamber pressure and is the last region to receive blood flow

choices.label: B
choices.text: The subendocardium has a lower density of mitochondria and therefore depends more on anaerobic glycolysis for energy production

choices.label: C
choices.text: Epicardial arteries supply the subendocardium first before reaching the epicardium, making the epicardium more susceptible to flow limitation

choices.label: D
choices.text: The subendocardium has fewer adrenergic receptors and therefore cannot mount an adequate vasodilatory response to ischemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Coronary venous drainage is impaired in the subendocardium due to compression by trabecular muscles during the cardiac cycle

explanation.summary: The subendocardium is the innermost layer of the myocardium and experiences the greatest compressive forces from ventricular contraction and chamber pressure during systole. It is also the last region to receive blood flow from the epicardial arteries that penetrate inward. These factors make it the most vulnerable region to ischemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: During systole, the subendocardial arteries experience greater compression from cardiac contraction and ventricular chamber pressure than epicardial vessels. The subendocardium is the last region to receive blood flow as arteries penetrate from the epicardial surface inward. These flow limitations make it most susceptible to ischemia, especially when perfusion pressure is compromised.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cardiac myocytes throughout the myocardium are rich in mitochondria and depend on aerobic metabolism. The subendocardium does not differ significantly in mitochondrial density from the epicardium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Blood flows from epicardial arteries through intramural arteries to the subendocardium—the subendocardium receives blood last, not first. The subendocardium, not epicardium, is more susceptible.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The vulnerability of the subendocardium is primarily due to mechanical compression during systole, not differences in adrenergic receptor density or vasodilatory capacity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: While venous drainage plays a role in tissue perfusion, the primary reason for subendocardial vulnerability is the greater systolic compression of arterial supply, not impaired venous drainage.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old athlete is performing high-intensity interval training. During peak exercise, his heart rate reaches 185/min and his cardiac output is 25 L/min. A sports medicine physician explains that despite maximal sympathetic activation causing alpha-1 mediated vasoconstriction in most vascular beds, coronary blood flow actually increases during exercise. Which of the following best explains this paradox?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Coronary arteries lack alpha-1 adrenergic receptors entirely and are therefore unaffected by sympathetic nervous system activation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Parasympathetic stimulation of muscarinic receptors on coronary vessels during exercise produces strong vasodilation that overrides sympathetic effects

choices.label: C
choices.text: Beta-1 adrenergic receptors on coronary artery smooth muscle directly cause vasodilation, counteracting the alpha-1 vasoconstrictor effect

choices.label: D
choices.text: The myogenic autoregulatory response to decreased diastolic pressure during tachycardia produces reflexive coronary vasodilation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Local metabolic vasodilators such as adenosine and nitric oxide override the relatively weak alpha-1 vasoconstrictor effect on coronary arteries

explanation.summary: While sympathetic activation stimulates alpha-1 receptors on coronary arteries causing vasoconstriction, this effect is minimal because coronary arteries have few alpha-1 receptors. More importantly, local metabolic vasodilators (adenosine, nitric oxide, low ATP) released during increased cardiac activity override this weak vasoconstrictive effect—a process called functional sympatholysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: During exercise, increased cardiac metabolic activity releases vasodilatory substances including adenosine, nitric oxide, and triggers KATP channel opening from low ATP. These metabolic vasodilators powerfully override the relatively weak alpha-1 vasoconstrictor effect on coronary arteries (functional sympatholysis), ensuring adequate coronary blood flow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Coronary arteries do have alpha-1 adrenergic receptors that cause vasoconstriction when stimulated. However, this effect is minimal compared to peripheral arteries and is overridden by local metabolic vasodilators.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Parasympathetic stimulation of muscarinic receptors on coronary vessels produces only slight vasodilation and is a minor effect. During exercise, parasympathetic tone is actually withdrawn, not increased.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Beta-1 receptors on the heart primarily affect contractility and heart rate of cardiomyocytes. Coronary vasodilation is mediated by beta-2 receptors on smaller resistance vessels and by metabolic vasodilators, not beta-1 receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The myogenic response causes vasoconstriction in response to increased pressure (stretch), not vasodilation. During exercise, the primary mechanism increasing coronary flow is metabolic vasodilation, not myogenic autoregulation.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with severe aortic stenosis presents with exertional angina despite angiographically normal coronary arteries. Which of the following best explains why this patient experiences myocardial ischemia in the absence of coronary artery disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aortic stenosis causes coronary artery vasospasm through a reflex arc involving aortic baroreceptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: The stenotic valve reduces coronary perfusion pressure while compensatory ventricular hypertrophy increases oxygen demand

choices.label: C
choices.text: Aortic stenosis increases coronary venous pressure through backward transmission of elevated left ventricular pressure

choices.label: D
choices.text: The turbulent flow across the stenotic valve damages coronary endothelium, impairing nitric oxide-mediated vasodilation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Aortic stenosis causes chronic tachycardia that shortens diastole and reduces coronary perfusion time

explanation.summary: Aortic stenosis creates a multifactorial threat to myocardial oxygen balance. The narrowed valve reduces coronary perfusion pressure while increasing left ventricular workload and oxygen demand. Compensatory left ventricular hypertrophy further increases oxygen requirements while compressing intramyocardial vessels, explaining angina even without coronary artery disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aortic stenosis increases left ventricular workload and oxygen demand while simultaneously reducing coronary perfusion pressure. The compensatory left ventricular hypertrophy increases oxygen requirements and compresses intramyocardial vessels. This combination of increased demand and compromised supply causes myocardial ischemia and angina even without coronary artery disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aortic stenosis does not cause coronary vasospasm through a baroreceptor reflex. The ischemia results from the combination of increased oxygen demand and reduced perfusion pressure, not vasospasm.
whyWrongByChoice.C: While elevated LVEDP can reduce the coronary perfusion gradient, the primary mechanism is not backward transmission of venous pressure but rather the combination of reduced perfusion pressure and increased demand from hypertrophy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Turbulent flow across the aortic valve does not directly damage coronary endothelium. The coronary ostia are located just above the valve, and the mechanism of ischemia is hemodynamic, not endothelial injury.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aortic stenosis does not typically cause chronic tachycardia as a primary mechanism. The ischemia is caused by the supply-demand mismatch from increased workload, hypertrophy, and reduced perfusion pressure.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man undergoes dobutamine stress echocardiography to evaluate suspected coronary artery disease. At peak dobutamine infusion, a new regional wall motion abnormality is detected in the anterior wall. His cardiologist explains the physiologic basis of this test. Which of the following best describes the principle underlying dobutamine stress testing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dobutamine causes direct coronary vasoconstriction that unmasks flow-limiting stenoses by reducing perfusion to at-risk territories

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dobutamine selectively dilates collateral blood vessels, redirecting flow away from territories supplied by stenotic arteries

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dobutamine decreases coronary perfusion pressure by reducing systemic vascular resistance, revealing areas with compromised autoregulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dobutamine increases cardiac workload and oxygen demand, unmasking regions supplied by stenotic vessels that cannot increase blood flow to meet demand

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dobutamine increases myocardial oxygen extraction ratio above the resting maximum, causing lactic acidosis in regions with borderline perfusion

explanation.summary: Dobutamine stress testing increases cardiac workload through positive inotropic and chronotropic effects (via beta receptor stimulation). This increases myocardial oxygen demand. Regions supplied by stenotic coronary arteries cannot adequately increase blood flow to meet the heightened demand, revealing ischemia as regional wall motion abnormalities.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dobutamine is a beta agonist with positive inotropic and chronotropic effects that increases cardiac workload and oxygen demand. This assesses coronary flow reserve: regions perfused by atherosclerotic vessels have minimal ability to dilate and increase flow to meet demand. The resulting ischemia manifests as wall motion abnormalities, unmasking critical coronary stenoses.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dobutamine does not cause direct coronary vasoconstriction. It is a beta agonist that increases cardiac workload. The test unmasks stenoses by increasing demand beyond the supply capacity of diseased vessels.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dobutamine does not selectively dilate collateral vessels. Coronary steal is associated with arteriolar vasodilators like adenosine, not dobutamine. Dobutamine increases workload to unmask flow-limiting stenoses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: While dobutamine may affect systemic hemodynamics, the principle of the test is increasing myocardial oxygen demand to unmask stenoses, not reducing coronary perfusion pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Myocardial oxygen extraction is already near-maximal (70-80%) at rest and cannot meaningfully increase further. The test principle is that stenotic vessels cannot increase flow to match increased demand.

questions.stem: A physiologist is studying the metabolic regulation of coronary blood flow. She observes that when myocardial oxygen consumption increases, coronary arteriolar resistance decreases rapidly. She identifies three key substances primarily responsible for this coronary vasodilation. Which of the following combinations best represents these three primary mediators?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Norepinephrine, angiotensin II, and endothelin-1

choices.label: B
choices.text: Histamine, serotonin, and prostaglandin F2-alpha

choices.label: C
choices.text: Adenosine, nitric oxide, and low ATP

choices.label: D
choices.text: Acetylcholine, bradykinin, and atrial natriuretic peptide

choices.label: E
choices.text: Carbon dioxide, hydrogen ions, and potassium ions

explanation.summary: The three primary mediators of metabolic coronary vasodilation are adenosine (a byproduct of ATP breakdown), nitric oxide (produced by endothelial cells in response to shear stress), and decreased ATP levels (which open ATP-sensitive potassium channels, causing smooth muscle hyperpolarization and vasodilation).
explanation.whyCorrect: The source identifies three key factors driving coronary dilation: (1) increased adenosine from ATP breakdown during high energy consumption, (2) increased nitric oxide from endothelial shear stress as cardiac output rises, and (3) decreased ATP opening KATP channels causing smooth muscle hyperpolarization and relaxation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Norepinephrine, angiotensin II, and endothelin-1 are all vasoconstrictors. They do not mediate the metabolic coronary vasodilation observed during increased myocardial oxygen consumption.
whyWrongByChoice.B: While histamine and serotonin can affect vascular tone, they are not the primary mediators of metabolic coronary vasodilation. Prostaglandin F2-alpha is a vasoconstrictor, not a vasodilator.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acetylcholine and bradykinin can cause vasodilation, but they are not the primary mediators of metabolic coronary blood flow regulation. Atrial natriuretic peptide affects renal sodium handling and is not a coronary metabolic vasodilator.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Carbon dioxide, hydrogen ions, and potassium are secondary factors that may contribute to coronary vasodilation, but they are not the three primary mediators. The source identifies adenosine, nitric oxide, and low ATP as the key drivers.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman with no prior cardiac history develops atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 162/min during a stressful business meeting. She presents to the emergency department with substernal chest discomfort. Her troponin is mildly elevated at 0.08 ng/mL. Coronary angiography performed the following day reveals no significant coronary artery disease. Which of the following best explains the mechanism by which tachycardia alone caused myocardial injury in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tachycardia increased coronary perfusion pressure above the autoregulatory range, causing endothelial damage and microhemorrhage

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tachycardia activated the parasympathetic nervous system, causing severe coronary vasospasm through muscarinic receptor stimulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tachycardia caused excessive coronary vasodilation through adenosine overproduction, leading to vascular steal from subendocardial regions

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tachycardia increased systemic venous return, raising left ventricular end-diastolic pressure and completely eliminating the coronary perfusion gradient

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rapid ventricular rate shortened diastole and reduced coronary perfusion time while simultaneously increasing myocardial oxygen demand from more frequent contractions

explanation.summary: Tachycardia causes a dual threat to myocardial oxygen balance. The rapid heart rate shortens diastole, the phase during which most coronary blood flow occurs, reducing oxygen supply. Simultaneously, the more frequent contractions increase myocardial oxygen demand. This supply-demand mismatch can cause ischemia and myocardial injury even without coronary artery disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: At a ventricular rate of 162/min, diastole is markedly shortened, dramatically reducing the time available for coronary perfusion (which occurs primarily during diastole). The increased number of contractions simultaneously raises oxygen demand. This double threat of reduced supply and increased demand causes myocardial ischemia and troponin elevation even in the absence of coronary disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Tachycardia does not typically increase coronary perfusion pressure above the autoregulatory range. The issue is reduced diastolic perfusion time and increased demand, not excessive perfusion pressure causing endothelial damage.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Tachycardia from atrial fibrillation is not caused by parasympathetic activation, and the parasympathetic system causes only slight vasodilation, not vasospasm, in coronary vessels.
whyWrongByChoice.C: While adenosine is released during increased metabolic demand, the primary mechanism of injury is the shortened diastolic perfusion time and increased oxygen demand, not coronary steal from adenosine overproduction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: While tachycardia may modestly increase LVEDP, it does not completely eliminate the coronary perfusion gradient. The primary mechanism is shortened diastole reducing perfusion time combined with increased oxygen consumption.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with a 30-pack-year smoking history and poorly controlled hypertension undergoes coronary catheterization after presenting with an acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Angiography reveals a ruptured plaque in the left anterior descending artery with an overlying thrombus. A biopsy of the plaque wall shows lipid-laden cells with a bubbly, vacuolated cytoplasm. Which of the following best describes the origin of these cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Monocytes that migrated into the intima and phagocytosed oxidized lipids

choices.label: B
choices.text: Smooth muscle cells that proliferated in response to platelet-derived growth factor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Endothelial cells that underwent apoptosis after exposure to reactive oxygen species

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fibroblasts that synthesized collagen to form the fibrous cap of the plaque

choices.label: E
choices.text: T lymphocytes that accumulated within the fatty streak during chronic inflammation

explanation.summary: Foam cells are lipid-laden macrophages formed when monocytes migrate into the intima, differentiate into macrophages, and phagocytose oxidized LDL.
explanation.whyCorrect: The bubbly, vacuolated cells described are foam cells. In atherosclerosis, endothelial damage increases permeability, allowing lipids to accumulate in the intima where they become oxidized. Monocytes recruited by cytokines enter the intima, differentiate into macrophages, and engulf the oxidized lipids, becoming foam cells with a characteristic bubbly appearance on histology.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Smooth muscle cells are recruited later in atheroma formation to cap the fatty streak and do not form the characteristic lipid-laden foam cells seen on histology.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Endothelial cells are damaged in the initial step of atherosclerosis but do not become the lipid-laden foam cells; endothelial injury triggers the inflammatory cascade that leads to foam cell formation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fibroblasts contribute to connective tissue in the fibrous cap but are not the lipid-laden cells with bubbly cytoplasm described in the question.
whyWrongByChoice.E: T lymphocytes are present in fatty streaks and contribute to inflammation, but the characteristic lipid-laden cells with vacuolated cytoplasm are macrophage-derived foam cells, not lymphocytes.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and hyperlipidemia presents to her primary care physician for a routine visit. She has no current complaints. Her physician counsels her about atherosclerosis risk. The physician explains that atherosclerosis begins much earlier in life than most patients realize. At what age does early atherosclerosis typically begin to develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In utero during the third trimester of fetal development

choices.label: B
choices.text: During childhood and adolescence, typically between ages 15 and 35 years

choices.label: C
choices.text: During early adulthood, typically between ages 35 and 45 years

choices.label: D
choices.text: During middle age, typically between ages 45 and 55 years

choices.label: E
choices.text: During late adulthood, typically after age 65 years

explanation.summary: Early atherosclerosis is present in nearly all people ages 15 to 35 years in the United States, beginning silently during childhood.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although atherosclerosis is often thought of as a disease of older age, the pathologic process actually begins silently during childhood. In the United States, early atherosclerosis is present in nearly all people ages 15 to 35 years, well before clinical symptoms manifest.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atherosclerosis does not begin in utero; although fetal endothelial cells are forming, the pathologic process of atheroma formation requires postnatal risk factor exposure and begins during childhood.
whyWrongByChoice.C: While atherosclerosis may become more clinically evident in early adulthood, the process begins much earlier, during childhood and adolescence.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Middle age is when atherosclerosis typically becomes clinically evident with symptoms, but the pathologic process has been developing silently for decades by that point.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Late adulthood is associated with advanced atherosclerotic disease and complications, but the underlying process began decades earlier during childhood.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with a history of smoking and hypertension dies suddenly while exercising. At autopsy, the pathologist identifies a large thrombus overlying a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque in a major coronary artery. The coronary arteries otherwise show only mild-to-moderate atherosclerosis. Which of the following best explains the mechanism by which plaque rupture led to thrombus formation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Release of tissue plasminogen activator from damaged endothelial cells activated the fibrinolytic cascade

choices.label: B
choices.text: Exposure of vascular smooth muscle triggered complement-mediated lysis of circulating erythrocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Exposure of subendothelial collagen to circulating platelets and clotting proteins initiated the coagulation cascade

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rupture of the plaque released cholesterol crystals that directly activated Factor XII in the intrinsic pathway

choices.label: E
choices.text: Disruption of laminar blood flow caused stasis and activation of the protein C anticoagulant pathway

explanation.summary: Plaque rupture exposes subendothelial collagen to platelets and clotting proteins, initiating thrombus formation that can rapidly occlude the artery.
explanation.whyCorrect: When the thin fibrous cap of an atherosclerotic plaque ruptures, the underlying endothelial collagen is exposed to circulating platelets and clotting proteins in the blood. This initiates platelet aggregation and thrombus formation, which can cause rapid arterial occlusion leading to myocardial infarction and sudden death.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Tissue plasminogen activator promotes fibrinolysis (clot breakdown), not clot formation; its release would counteract rather than promote thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Complement-mediated erythrocyte lysis is not the mechanism of thrombus formation after plaque rupture; the key event is platelet activation upon collagen exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: While cholesterol crystals can embolize from ruptured plaques, the primary mechanism of thrombus formation is exposure of subendothelial collagen to platelets and clotting factors, not direct Factor XII activation by cholesterol.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Protein C is an anticoagulant pathway that inhibits clotting; disruption of laminar flow contributes to endothelial damage but does not activate an anticoagulant pathway to form thrombi.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with a history of diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia presents with cramping pain in both calves that occurs after walking two blocks and resolves with rest. Physical examination reveals diminished pedal pulses bilaterally. Which of the following best describes the pathologic process causing this patient's symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Venous insufficiency causing blood pooling and tissue edema in the lower extremities

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autoimmune vasculitis with granulomatous inflammation of medium-sized arteries

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vasospasm of peripheral arteries triggered by cold exposure and sympathetic activation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deep venous thrombosis with retrograde venous flow and valvular incompetence

choices.label: E
choices.text: Atherosclerotic narrowing of peripheral arteries causing tissue ischemia during exertion

explanation.summary: Intermittent claudication is exertional leg pain caused by atherosclerotic narrowing of peripheral arteries that limits blood flow during activity.
explanation.whyCorrect: This patient presents with classic intermittent claudication—cramping leg pain with exertion that resolves with rest—a hallmark of peripheral artery disease (PAD). Atherosclerosis in the peripheral arteries, especially the legs, narrows the arterial lumen, restricting blood flow. During exertion, the increased oxygen demand cannot be met, producing ischemic pain that resolves when demand decreases at rest.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Venous insufficiency causes edema, skin changes, and aching that worsens with standing, not the exertional cramping pain with diminished pulses seen in this patient.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Autoimmune vasculitis (such as polyarteritis nodosa) can affect medium arteries but typically presents with systemic symptoms, skin lesions, and organ involvement rather than classic intermittent claudication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vasospasm of peripheral arteries (as in Raynaud phenomenon) typically affects the digits and is triggered by cold, not exertion, and presents with color changes rather than calf cramping.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Deep venous thrombosis presents with unilateral leg swelling, warmth, and pain, not bilateral exertional cramping relieved by rest with diminished arterial pulses.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with known atherosclerotic disease undergoes Doppler ultrasonography of the lower extremities, which reveals significant stenosis of the right femoral artery. His physician prescribes a statin medication. In addition to lowering LDL cholesterol, which of the following is another beneficial effect of statin therapy in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct thrombolysis of existing arterial thrombi overlying atherosclerotic plaques

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inhibition of vascular smooth muscle proliferation in the tunica media of affected arteries

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reversal of existing arterial calcification within established atherosclerotic plaques

choices.label: D
choices.text: Plaque stabilization and decreased endothelial cell dysfunction in affected arteries

choices.label: E
choices.text: Direct vasodilation of stenotic arterial segments to immediately restore blood flow

explanation.summary: In addition to reducing circulating cholesterol and LDL-C levels, statins provide plaque stabilization and decrease endothelial cell dysfunction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Statins have pleiotropic effects beyond cholesterol reduction. They stabilize existing atherosclerotic plaques, making them less prone to rupture, and decrease endothelial cell dysfunction. These additional benefits contribute to reduced cardiovascular events.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Statins do not have thrombolytic activity; thrombolysis requires specific fibrinolytic agents such as tissue plasminogen activator (tPA).
whyWrongByChoice.B: While statins may have some anti-proliferative effects, their primary recognized benefits beyond lipid lowering are plaque stabilization and improvement of endothelial function, not direct inhibition of smooth muscle proliferation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Statins do not reverse existing arterial calcification; regression of atherosclerosis takes 12-24 months and involves slowing progression rather than reversing calcification.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Statins do not cause direct vasodilation; medications like nitrates and calcium channel blockers provide vasodilatory effects.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman presents to her cardiologist for evaluation of newly diagnosed coronary artery disease. She has no prior history of heart disease and is surprised by the diagnosis. Her physician explains that her risk increased significantly after menopause. Which of the following best explains the mechanism by which menopause increases atherosclerosis risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Estrogen deficiency leads to unfavorable cholesterol changes, increased arterial stiffness, and endothelial dysfunction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of estrogen leads to increased platelet aggregation and accelerated thrombus formation on intact endothelium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased progesterone levels after menopause directly promote foam cell formation in the coronary intima

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decreased follicle-stimulating hormone after menopause reduces hepatic clearance of circulating low-density lipoproteins

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of estrogen causes direct smooth muscle cell apoptosis in the coronary arterial wall leading to plaque instability

explanation.summary: Menopause increases atherosclerosis risk through estrogen deficiency, which causes unfavorable cholesterol changes, increased arterial stiffness, and endothelial dysfunction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Estrogen has protective cardiovascular effects. After menopause, estrogen deficiency leads to unfavorable changes in cholesterol levels (increased LDL, decreased HDL), increased arterial stiffness, and endothelial dysfunction—all of which accelerate atherosclerosis development.

whyWrongByChoice.C: Progesterone levels decrease, not increase, after menopause; progesterone does not directly promote foam cell formation in the mechanism described for postmenopausal atherosclerosis risk.
whyWrongByChoice.B: While estrogen loss affects cardiovascular health, the primary mechanism is through cholesterol changes, arterial stiffness, and endothelial dysfunction, not direct promotion of platelet aggregation on intact endothelium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: FSH actually increases after menopause, not decreases; the mechanism of increased atherosclerosis risk is related to estrogen deficiency, not changes in FSH affecting hepatic lipoprotein clearance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Estrogen deficiency does not cause direct smooth muscle cell apoptosis in coronary arteries; the mechanism involves systemic metabolic and vascular changes rather than direct cellular death.

questions.stem: A pathologist examines a section of the aorta from a 45-year-old man who died in a motor vehicle accident. Histologic examination reveals clusters of lipid-laden cells beneath the endothelium, along with scattered T cells and smooth muscle cells. No fibrous cap or calcification is present. Which of the following stages of atherosclerotic plaque development is best represented by these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endothelial injury response with monocyte recruitment and adhesion molecule expression

choices.label: B
choices.text: Foam cell formation with initial lipid accumulation beneath the endothelium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Smooth muscle recruitment with formation of a thin fibrous cap over the lesion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fatty streak formation with clustered foam cells, T cells, and smooth muscle cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transformation to atherosclerotic plaque with calcification and luminal narrowing

explanation.summary: Fatty streaks are the first visible atherosclerotic lesions on microscopy, composed of clustered foam cells along with T cells, platelets, and smooth muscle cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The histologic findings describe a fatty streak—clusters of lipid-laden foam cells with T cells and smooth muscle cells, without a fibrous cap or calcification. Fatty streaks are formed when foam cells accumulate and cluster, representing the first visible atherosclerotic regions on microscopy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The endothelial injury response involves cytokine release and monocyte recruitment but does not yet show the clustered lipid-laden cells, T cells, and smooth muscle cells described in this specimen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Foam cell formation involves individual macrophages engulfing oxidized lipids, but the clustering of these cells with T cells and smooth muscle cells indicates progression to the fatty streak stage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Smooth muscle recruitment with fibrous cap formation occurs after the fatty streak stage; this specimen lacks a fibrous cap, placing it at an earlier stage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transformation to an atherosclerotic plaque involves calcification, which is absent in this specimen, indicating the lesion has not yet progressed to this advanced stage.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with a history of smoking and hyperlipidemia presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of left-sided weakness and slurred speech. CT angiography of the head and neck reveals a 90% stenosis of the right internal carotid artery. Which of the following is the most likely source of this patient's neurological symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Embolization of cholesterol crystals from a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque to cerebral vessels

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vasospasm of the middle cerebral artery caused by sympathetic nervous system hyperactivation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemorrhagic transformation of a pre-existing lacunar infarct in the basal ganglia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Venous sinus thrombosis caused by hypercoagulability from chronic inflammatory state

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dissection of the vertebral artery with subsequent posterior circulation ischemia

explanation.summary: Atheroemboli from ruptured plaques can release cholesterol crystals that embolize to smaller cerebral arteries, causing stroke.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the setting of severe carotid atherosclerosis, plaque rupture can release cholesterol crystals and thrombus fragments that embolize downstream to cerebral vessels, causing ischemic stroke. This is a well-recognized complication of carotid atherosclerosis and explains the sudden-onset focal neurological deficits.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Vasospasm of cerebral arteries is typically associated with subarachnoid hemorrhage, not atherosclerotic carotid disease; the 90% carotid stenosis points to an atheroembolic source.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemorrhagic transformation of a lacunar infarct would not be the primary event in a patient with severe carotid stenosis presenting with acute neurological deficits consistent with anterior circulation ischemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Venous sinus thrombosis presents with headache, papilledema, and seizures rather than the acute focal deficits seen with arterial ischemia from carotid atherosclerosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vertebral artery dissection affects the posterior circulation; this patient's symptoms (left-sided weakness, slurred speech) with right carotid stenosis are more consistent with anterior circulation atheroembolism.

questions.stem: A researcher is studying the early steps of atheroma formation in a mouse model. Endothelial cells in the aorta of the experimental mice show increased expression of vascular cell adhesion molecules (VCAMs) and release of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Which of the following is the primary purpose of VCAM expression in the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To promote smooth muscle cell migration from the tunica media to the intima for fibrous cap formation

choices.label: B
choices.text: To facilitate oxidation of low-density lipoprotein particles within the subendothelial space

choices.label: C
choices.text: To increase endothelial permeability allowing red blood cell extravasation into the vessel wall

choices.label: D
choices.text: To stimulate platelet degranulation and initiate the extrinsic coagulation cascade

choices.label: E
choices.text: To enable monocyte adhesion to and infiltration of the damaged endothelium

explanation.summary: VCAMs are adhesion molecules produced by endothelial cells that allow monocytes to adhere to and infiltrate the endothelium during the inflammatory response to injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: In response to endothelial injury, endothelial cells release cytokines to recruit monocytes and produce adhesion molecules such as VCAMs. These adhesion molecules allow monocytes to adhere to the endothelial surface and then infiltrate through the endothelium as part of the inflammatory reparative process—a critical early step in atheroma formation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Smooth muscle cell migration occurs later in atheroma formation (Step 5) and is driven by growth factors, not by VCAM expression on endothelial cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: LDL oxidation occurs in the subendothelial space after lipids penetrate through the damaged endothelium; VCAMs facilitate immune cell adhesion rather than lipid oxidation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: While endothelial damage does increase permeability, VCAMs specifically facilitate leukocyte (particularly monocyte) adhesion, not red blood cell extravasation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelet degranulation and coagulation cascade activation occur during thrombus formation after plaque rupture, which is a later complication; VCAMs are involved in early monocyte recruitment.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man with a history of hypertension and smoking presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain. Physical examination reveals a pulsatile abdominal mass. CT angiography shows a 7-cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm with signs of contained rupture. Which of the following best describes the pathophysiologic mechanism by which atherosclerosis contributed to aneurysm formation at this location?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic inflammation from atherosclerosis caused fibrinoid necrosis and transmural vessel wall destruction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Atherosclerotic plaques caused turbulent blood flow that weakened and dilated the vessel wall

choices.label: C
choices.text: Atherosclerotic plaques directly eroded through the tunica media causing a pseudoaneurysm

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cholesterol crystal embolization from upstream plaques obstructed the vasa vasorum of the aorta

choices.label: E
choices.text: Atherosclerosis-induced endothelial dysfunction allowed blood to dissect between the intima and media

explanation.summary: Atheromas protrude into the vessel lumen, converting normal laminar flow to turbulent flow that injures, weakens, and dilates the vessel wall, leading to aneurysm formation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Atherosclerotic plaques protrude into the vessel lumen, causing normal laminar blood flow to become turbulent. This turbulent flow injures the vessel wall, which can weaken and dilate over time, forming an aneurysm. Aneurysms most often occur at arterial branch points, including the abdominal aorta.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fibrinoid necrosis is characteristic of malignant hypertension and certain vasculitides, not the typical mechanism of atherosclerosis-related aneurysm formation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Atherosclerotic plaques form in the intima and do not directly erode through the media to form pseudoaneurysms; the mechanism involves turbulent flow weakening the entire wall.
whyWrongByChoice.D: While cholesterol crystals can embolize from ruptured plaques, obstruction of the vasa vasorum is not the primary mechanism of atherosclerosis-related aortic aneurysm formation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aortic dissection involves blood tracking between vessel wall layers and is a distinct pathology from aneurysm formation; atherosclerosis-related aneurysms develop from wall weakening due to turbulent flow.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with hypercholesterolemia and a strong family history of premature coronary artery disease asks his physician about the most important risk factor for developing atherosclerosis. The physician explains that while modifiable risk factors are important to address, one non-modifiable factor stands out as the most significant independent predictor. Which of the following is the most important independent risk factor for atherosclerosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hypertension requiring multi-drug antihypertensive therapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Male sex with testosterone-mediated endothelial dysfunction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Diabetes mellitus with chronic hyperglycemia and insulin resistance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increasing age with progressive accumulation of atherosclerotic plaques

choices.label: E
choices.text: Family history of premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease

explanation.summary: Family history (genetics) is the most important independent risk factor for atherosclerosis among the non-modifiable constitutional risk factors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Family history is identified as the most important independent risk factor for atherosclerosis. Genetic predisposition plays a major role in determining an individual's susceptibility to atherosclerotic disease, independent of modifiable risk factors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hypertension is a major modifiable risk factor for atherosclerosis but is not the most important independent risk factor; it can be addressed with lifestyle changes and medications.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Male sex is a non-modifiable risk factor, but family history is considered the most important independent risk factor; additionally, the sex-based risk difference diminishes after women reach menopause.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Diabetes mellitus is a major modifiable risk factor but is not classified as the most important independent risk factor for atherosclerosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increasing age is a non-modifiable risk factor that reflects the progressive nature of atherosclerotic plaque development, but family history is considered the most important independent risk factor.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with peripheral artery disease undergoes conventional arterial angiography of the right lower extremity. The angiogram reveals multiple areas of luminal narrowing in the right iliac and femoral arteries. Her physician recommends initiating statin therapy. After how many months can regression of atherosclerosis typically be expected with statin treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1 to 3 months after initiation of statin therapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: 3 to 6 months after initiation of statin therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: 12 to 24 months after initiation of statin therapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: 6 to 9 months after initiation of statin therapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: 36 to 48 months after initiation of statin therapy

explanation.summary: The regression of atherosclerosis with statin therapy typically takes 12 to 24 months.
explanation.whyCorrect: Statins decrease circulating cholesterol and LDL-C levels, slow progression of cholesterol deposition, provide plaque stabilization, and decrease endothelial dysfunction. However, actual regression of atherosclerosis is a slow process that typically requires 12 to 24 months of statin therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: One to three months is too early to expect regression of atherosclerosis; while cholesterol levels may improve quickly, structural changes in plaques take much longer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Three to six months is insufficient time for atherosclerosis regression, although beneficial effects on lipid levels and some plaque stabilization may begin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Six to nine months is still earlier than the typical timeframe for atherosclerosis regression, which requires 12 to 24 months.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thirty-six to 48 months overestimates the time needed; regression can typically be observed within 12 to 24 months of statin therapy.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with coronary artery disease undergoes coronary artery biopsy during a catheterization procedure. Histologic examination reveals cholesterol clefts within the intimal layer of the vessel. Which of the following best describes the process that leads to cholesterol cleft formation within an atherosclerotic lesion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Precipitation of circulating LDL cholesterol directly into the subendothelial space through damaged endothelium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Apoptosis of lipid-laden foam cells leaving behind residual lipid deposits that fill the spaces of dead cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Active secretion of cholesterol esters by smooth muscle cells recruited to form the fibrous cap

choices.label: D
choices.text: Calcium-mediated transformation of fatty streaks into calcified atheromatous plaques

choices.label: E
choices.text: Endothelial cell necrosis releasing intracellular cholesterol stores into the vessel wall matrix

explanation.summary: Cholesterol clefts form when foam cells undergo apoptosis and the lipids they contained remain behind, filling the spaces left by the dead cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: During fatty streak formation, foam cells (lipid-laden macrophages) eventually undergo apoptosis. The lipids they had phagocytosed remain behind, filling the spaces formed by the apoptotic cells. These residual lipid deposits are known as cholesterol clefts and may appear in the intima or tunica media.

whyWrongByChoice.A: While lipids do enter through damaged endothelium, cholesterol clefts specifically result from foam cell apoptosis leaving residual lipids, not from direct precipitation of circulating LDL.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Smooth muscle cells are recruited to form the fibrous cap but do not actively secrete cholesterol esters to form cholesterol clefts; the clefts derive from apoptotic foam cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Calcification is a later step in atherosclerotic plaque transformation and is distinct from cholesterol cleft formation, which occurs during the fatty streak stage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Endothelial cells are damaged in the early steps of atherosclerosis, but cholesterol clefts arise from apoptotic foam cells (macrophage-derived), not from endothelial cell necrosis.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis, subclinical hypothyroidism, and gout presents for cardiovascular risk assessment. She does not smoke, has normal blood pressure, and has well-controlled blood glucose. Her physician explains that some of her medical conditions may contribute to atherosclerosis risk. Which of the following best categorizes these conditions in terms of atherosclerosis risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are major modifiable risk factors equivalent to hypertension and diabetes

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are non-modifiable constitutional risk factors similar to age and sex

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are disorders that may serve as minor risk factors for atherosclerosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: They are protective factors that decrease the progression of atherosclerotic disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: They have no established association with atherosclerosis development or progression

explanation.summary: Rheumatoid arthritis, subclinical hypothyroidism, and gout are classified as disorders that may be minor risk factors for atherosclerosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rheumatoid arthritis, gout, and subclinical hypothyroidism (or hyperthyroidism) are listed among disorders that may serve as risk factors for atherosclerosis. They are classified separately from the major modifiable risk factors (smoking, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, obesity) and the non-modifiable constitutional factors (genetics, age, sex).

whyWrongByChoice.A: These conditions are not classified as major modifiable risk factors; major modifiable risk factors include hypertension, diabetes, smoking, dyslipidemia, and abdominal obesity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: These are not non-modifiable constitutional risk factors; constitutional risk factors include genetics/family history, increasing age, and male gender.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These conditions are associated with increased, not decreased, atherosclerosis risk; chronic inflammation and metabolic derangements from these conditions may contribute to accelerated atherogenesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These conditions do have established associations with atherosclerosis; they are specifically listed as disorders that may serve as risk factors.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man with a history of chronic atrial fibrillation presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of severe left leg pain that began 3 hours ago while sitting in his recliner. On examination, the left foot is pale and cool to touch. No dorsalis pedis or posterior tibial pulses are palpable on the left side. The patient reports numbness in the left foot and is unable to dorsiflex the ankle. Which of the following best describes the origin of the material most likely responsible for this patient's presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Thrombus formed in the left atrium due to blood stasis from loss of coordinated atrial contraction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cholesterol crystals dislodged from an atherosclerotic plaque in the abdominal aorta during catheterization

choices.label: C
choices.text: Venous thrombus from the lower extremity that crossed through a patent foramen ovale to the arterial side

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fat globules released into the circulation following a long bone fracture sustained during a recent fall

choices.label: E
choices.text: Platelet-rich thrombus formed at the site of a ruptured coronary artery atherosclerotic plaque

explanation.summary: Atrial fibrillation is the most common single cause of arterial thromboemboli. AF leads to loss of atrial contraction, promoting blood stasis and thrombus formation in the left atrium. The thrombus can then embolize to distant arteries, causing acute limb ischemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The patient has known atrial fibrillation, which is the most common cause of arterial thromboemboli. AF causes loss of coordinated atrial contraction, leading to blood stasis in the left atrium, which promotes thrombus formation. Fragments of this thrombus can embolize to the lower extremity, producing the 6 Ps of acute limb ischemia seen here (pain, pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paresthesia, paralysis).

whyWrongByChoice.B: Atheroemboli are composed of cholesterol crystals from atherosclerotic plaques and account for only 1-3% of arterial emboli. They are typically multiple and small, lodging in small vessels, and are usually associated with intravascular procedures rather than occurring spontaneously in this clinical setting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Paradoxical embolism from the venous system requires a congenital intracardiac shunt such as a patent foramen ovale. There is no history suggesting a right-to-left shunt, and this is a much less common mechanism than direct thromboembolism from atrial fibrillation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fat emboli are associated with long bone fractures and are a rare type of arterial embolus. There is no history of trauma or fracture in this patient, making this an unlikely source.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A ruptured coronary plaque would cause a local coronary event such as myocardial infarction, not a peripheral arterial embolism to the lower extremity. The clinical presentation points to a proximal embolic source rather than a coronary event.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man undergoes a diagnostic arteriogram for evaluation of peripheral arterial disease. Two days later, he presents with painful, cyanotic toes on both feet, a lacy purplish reticular rash on his lower extremities, and mildly elevated serum creatinine. His peripheral pulses remain palpable bilaterally. Laboratory studies show elevated eosinophil count and decreased serum complement. Which of the following best explains the pathophysiology of this patient's condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single large thrombus formed in the left atrium and embolized to the bilateral femoral arteries simultaneously

choices.label: B
choices.text: Multiple small cholesterol crystals were dislodged from atherosclerotic plaques by the catheter

choices.label: C
choices.text: A deep vein thrombus traveled through a patent foramen ovale and lodged in the bilateral popliteal arteries

choices.label: D
choices.text: An acute inflammatory vasculitis developed as an allergic reaction to the contrast dye used during the arteriogram

choices.label: E
choices.text: Air introduced during the arteriography procedure formed bubbles that occluded small arteries in the feet and kidneys

explanation.summary: Atheroemboli are composed of tiny cholesterol crystals that break off from atherosclerotic plaques, often following intravascular procedures such as arteriography. They tend to be multiple (causing an 'embolism shower'), lodge in small vessels, and can produce livedo reticularis, blue toe syndrome, renal insufficiency, eosinophilia, and decreased complement.
explanation.whyCorrect: The temporal relationship with arteriography, bilateral involvement, preserved pulses (indicating small vessel disease), livedo reticularis, blue toes, renal dysfunction, eosinophilia, and decreased complement are all classic for atheroembolism. Intravascular procedures are the most common cause of plaque destabilization leading to cholesterol crystal embolization to small distal vessels.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thromboemboli from the left atrium are typically single and large, lodging in medium to large vessels and causing pulselessness distal to the occlusion. This patient has palpable pulses and bilateral small-vessel involvement, which is inconsistent with a single large thromboembolus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Paradoxical embolism requires a congenital intracardiac shunt and typically produces single-vessel occlusion rather than the diffuse bilateral small-vessel disease pattern seen here with preserved peripheral pulses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Contrast allergy can cause urticaria, bronchospasm, and anaphylaxis, but it does not cause the localized ischemic changes in toes, livedo reticularis, or the specific laboratory pattern of eosinophilia with decreased complement seen in atheroembolism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Air embolism during arteriography is extremely rare with modern techniques and would not produce the delayed onset, bilateral small vessel occlusion pattern, livedo reticularis, or the characteristic laboratory findings of eosinophilia and hypocomplementemia.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset severe abdominal pain that began 4 hours ago. She has a history of atrial fibrillation and hypertension. Her vital signs show a heart rate of 120 beats/min and an irregularly irregular rhythm. On physical examination, her abdomen is soft and nontender with no guarding, rigidity, or rebound tenderness. Bowel sounds are hypoactive. Serum lactate level is elevated. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute appendicitis with early peritonitis and localized peritoneal inflammation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Perforated duodenal ulcer with free air causing diffuse peritoneal irritation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Acute cholecystitis with gallbladder distension and right upper quadrant tenderness

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mesenteric ischemia from arterial embolization to the superior mesenteric artery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Small bowel obstruction from adhesions causing colicky intermittent abdominal pain

explanation.summary: Mesenteric ischemia classically presents with severe abdominal pain that is 'out of proportion' to physical exam findings. The combination of atrial fibrillation as an embolic source, sudden severe pain, benign abdominal exam, and elevated lactate strongly suggests an arterial embolus to the mesenteric circulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: This patient has the classic presentation of mesenteric ischemia from arterial embolization: severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical findings, atrial fibrillation as the embolic source, and elevated serum lactate from ischemic tissue switching to anaerobic metabolism. The deceptively normal abdominal exam is a hallmark of mesenteric ischemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute appendicitis typically presents with localized right lower quadrant tenderness, guarding, and rebound tenderness on exam. The absence of peritoneal signs despite severe pain makes appendicitis unlikely.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A perforated duodenal ulcer causes diffuse peritonitis with a rigid, board-like abdomen, guarding, and rebound tenderness. The soft, nontender abdomen in this patient is inconsistent with perforation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acute cholecystitis presents with right upper quadrant tenderness and a positive Murphy sign. The patient's exam shows no localized tenderness, which is inconsistent with cholecystitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Small bowel obstruction from adhesions causes colicky, intermittent pain with abdominal distension and hyperactive (not hypoactive) bowel sounds. The pattern of constant severe pain with a benign exam is more consistent with mesenteric ischemia.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with atrial fibrillation presents with acute right arm pain and weakness. CT angiography reveals complete occlusion of the right brachial artery by a thromboembolus. The arm is pale, cool, and pulseless distal to the mid-upper arm. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management for this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Long-term oral warfarin therapy to prevent further thromboembolic events

choices.label: B
choices.text: Statin therapy combined with smoking cessation counseling and blood pressure control

choices.label: C
choices.text: Systemic anticoagulation with heparin alone and serial monitoring of the limb

choices.label: D
choices.text: Surgical thrombectomy or thrombolytic therapy to restore blood flow to the limb

choices.label: E
choices.text: Endovascular endarterectomy with stent placement at the site of arterial occlusion

explanation.summary: A totally occluded artery from a thromboembolus requires revascularization to restore blood flow. This is typically accomplished by open surgical thrombectomy or thrombolytic therapy. Total occlusion can result in limb loss if not treated urgently.
explanation.whyCorrect: In arterial thromboembolic disease with total occlusion, the immediate goal is revascularization to restore blood flow and prevent limb loss. This is achieved through surgical thrombectomy or thrombolytic therapy (e.g., tissue plasminogen activator). The patient has signs of complete occlusion (pallor, coolness, pulselessness), making urgent intervention necessary.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Long-term warfarin therapy is important for preventing future thromboembolic events from atrial fibrillation, but it does not address the acute total occlusion. Warfarin alone cannot restore blood flow to a completely occluded artery.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Statin therapy, smoking cessation, and blood pressure control are the cornerstones of atheroemboli management, not acute thromboembolism with total occlusion. These measures address atherosclerotic risk factors rather than an acute thrombotic event.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Systemic anticoagulation with heparin is appropriate for partial arterial occlusion to prevent clot enlargement, but it is insufficient for total occlusion where there is no blood flow and imminent risk of limb loss.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Endovascular endarterectomy with stenting is used for atheroembolic disease to remove the atherosclerotic source. This is not the appropriate initial treatment for an acute thromboembolus causing complete vessel occlusion.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with a history of a patent foramen ovale diagnosed incidentally on echocardiogram 5 years ago presents with sudden-onset left-sided hemiparesis and aphasia. A CT of the head shows no hemorrhage. CT angiography demonstrates occlusion of the right middle cerebral artery. A lower extremity duplex ultrasound reveals a thrombus in the right femoral vein. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which a venous thrombus caused this patient's stroke?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The venous thrombus traveled to the pulmonary arteries, causing pulmonary hypertension and secondary cerebral hypoperfusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: The venous thrombus released inflammatory cytokines that triggered de novo thrombus formation in the cerebral arterial circulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: The venous thrombus embolized through the patent foramen ovale from the right atrium to the left atrium and then to the cerebral artery

choices.label: D
choices.text: The venous thrombus traveled retrograde through the jugular venous system to directly enter the cerebral venous sinuses and arteries

choices.label: E
choices.text: The venous thrombus caused systemic activation of the coagulation cascade leading to disseminated intravascular coagulation and stroke

explanation.summary: A paradoxical embolism occurs when a venous thrombus crosses from the right side of the heart to the left side through a congenital intracardiac shunt (most commonly a patent foramen ovale), bypassing the lung capillary bed and entering the arterial circulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The patient has a known patent foramen ovale (PFO), which is the most common congenital intracardiac shunt allowing paradoxical embolism. A thrombus from the femoral vein traveled through the inferior vena cava to the right atrium, crossed through the PFO to the left atrium, and then embolized to the right middle cerebral artery causing stroke.

whyWrongByChoice.A: While pulmonary embolism from a venous thrombus can cause hemodynamic compromise, it would not selectively occlude a cerebral artery. The CT angiography shows a focal right MCA occlusion, which requires a direct embolic mechanism rather than global hypoperfusion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Venous thrombi do not cause de novo arterial thrombus formation through cytokine release. The presence of a documented femoral vein thrombus and a PFO provides a direct embolic pathway that explains the focal cerebral artery occlusion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Venous blood does not flow retrograde from the systemic veins into the cerebral circulation. The normal direction of venous flow carries blood toward the heart, and there is no anatomic pathway for retrograde venous-to-arterial access in the brain.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Disseminated intravascular coagulation would cause widespread microvascular thrombosis and bleeding, not a single focal arterial occlusion of the middle cerebral artery. The clinical presentation is consistent with a focal embolic event, not DIC.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man presents with sudden painless loss of vision in his left eye that began 1 hour ago. He has a history of atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. On funduscopic examination, the optic disk appears pale, and a cherry-red spot is visible on the macula. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's visual loss?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vitreous hemorrhage from proliferative diabetic retinopathy causing sudden visual obstruction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acute angle-closure glaucoma causing elevated intraocular pressure and optic nerve damage

choices.label: C
choices.text: Central retinal vein occlusion from venous thrombosis causing retinal edema and hemorrhages

choices.label: D
choices.text: Optic neuritis from demyelinating disease causing inflammation of the optic nerve sheath

choices.label: E
choices.text: Embolic occlusion of the central retinal artery from a thrombus originating in the left atrium
